M-ACE supports rapid functional staging across the AD continuum

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective diagnostic and staging study•October 8, 2026

M-ACE supports rapid functional staging across the AD continuum

In 1,834 consecutive patients, the Mini-Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination closely tracked the full ACE-III (ρ=0.822), outperformed MMSE at the subjective-decline-to-MCI transition and yielded stage-specific cutoffs, but retrospective FAST-based classification does not establish etiologic Alzheimer diagnosis or treatment eligibility.

Key quantitative results: M-ACE showed good internal consistency (McDonald's ω=0.835; Cronbach's α=0.731) and strong convergence with ACE-III (Spearman ρ=0.822).

ManagementCognitive screening

Added October 8, 2026 · DOI:10.5603/pjnns.113649; PMID:42841817

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

This large clinic cohort gives M-ACE a more specific role than generic screening: rapid follow-up and functional-stage discrimination, particularly early in the continuum. ACE-III remained the most consistently accurate instrument across transitions, while M-ACE lost discrimination later as memory recall reached a floor. The cutoffs are cohort-derived aids, not standalone diagnoses, biomarker substitutes or prescribing thresholds.

Study design

Investigators retrospectively analyzed 1,834 consecutive people seeking cognitive evaluation and classified them as subjective cognitive decline (FAST 2), mild cognitive impairment (FAST 3) or Alzheimer dementia (FAST 4-6). They compared M-ACE, ACE-III and MMSE using reliability, convergent validity, ROC analyses, optimal cutoffs, DeLong tests and stage-adjusted logistic regression.

Key quantitative results

  • M-ACE showed good internal consistency (McDonald's ω=0.835; Cronbach's α=0.731) and strong convergence with ACE-III (Spearman ρ=0.822).
  • M-ACE significantly outperformed MMSE for the FAST 2-to-3 transition and remained independently associated with stage after adjustment for age, sex and education. ACE-III had the most consistently high accuracy across transitions; MMSE had the highest AUC at FAST 4-to-5, but not significantly higher than ACE-III.
  • Optimal M-ACE cutoffs were ≤25 for FAST 2-to-3, ≤19 for FAST 3-to-4, ≤13 for FAST 4-to-5 and ≤7 for FAST 5-to-6. Memory Recall developed a floor effect from FAST 4, helping explain M-ACE's weaker late-stage discrimination.

What changed

The study supplies a large, stage-specific comparison of M-ACE, ACE-III and MMSE and proposes operational M-ACE thresholds for rapid longitudinal follow-up across the functional Alzheimer continuum.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity evidence for functional-stage discrimination in the studied referral cohort: large consecutive sample, direct instrument comparison and adjusted analyses are strengths. Retrospective design, cohort-derived cutoffs and FAST-based classification limit causal interpretation, external transportability and use for etiologic diagnosis.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

M-ACE may be a practical short instrument for repeated cognitive assessment when a full ACE-III is not feasible, especially around the subjective-decline-to-MCI transition. It should complement history, function, neurologic evaluation and indicated biomarker testing rather than determine an Alzheimer etiology or disease-modifying-treatment eligibility alone.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to memory-clinic workflow, stage documentation and selection of brief follow-up tools. It also reinforces the distinction between cognitive/functional staging and biological confirmation of Alzheimer pathology.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The study creates no new test authorization, commercial availability, guideline endorsement, reimbursement or coverage. M-ACE is a cognitive instrument; local licensing, language validation, training and workflow determine implementation.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can the proposed M-ACE cutoffs diagnose Alzheimer disease?
No. They discriminate FAST transitions in this retrospective clinical cohort. They do not establish Alzheimer etiology or replace amyloid confirmation when treatment or another decision requires it.
Is M-ACE better than ACE-III?
Not overall. ACE-III was the most consistently accurate across stages. M-ACE offered a useful balance of speed and accuracy, particularly at earlier transitions and for follow-up.
Does this change authorization, endorsement or coverage?
No. It is a performance study, not a regulatory action, formal guideline or payer decision.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-system clinical cohort
  • Stage classification was based on FAST rather than a uniform biomarker reference standard
  • Cutoffs were derived in the same clinical population and need external validation
  • The public report does not establish prospective management or patient-outcome benefit
  • M-ACE memory recall showed a floor effect from FAST stage 4
  • Results do not define anti-amyloid treatment eligibility

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record
